surfaces.label: All 217 tracked repository files
surfaces.notes: Independent baseline and focused parser review reconciled against git ls-files at c45eb915f63b0855988eca9d9c1bcb01dc42b86e; 217/217 fully reviewed, no excluded tracked files. Parent validated material trust-boundary conclusions against consumers. Complete refers to source coverage, not all-platform runtime assurance.

resolvedQuestions.question: Was the complete tracked scope reviewed, and what does the result establish?
resolvedQuestions.resolution: Fully reviewed all 217 tracked files at c45eb915f63b0855988eca9d9c1bcb01dc42b86e: 133 production source/resource/project files, 51 test/support/fixture files, 2 scripts, 2 workflows, and 29 documentation/root configuration files. The single binary fixture was inspected completely as 359 bytes of data. SECURITY.md resolution across all 62 tracked-file directories found no applicable guidance. Final tracked diff was empty. No defensible source-backed vulnerability with a meaningful attacker-controlled boundary crossing was established. This is a static analysis result, not a guarantee of absence; this worker did not run the application, tests, dependency scanners, network requests, or exploit probes.

resolvedQuestions.question: Can Steam metadata inject arbitrary commands through game launch or installation?
resolvedQuestions.resolution: No attacker-controlled command path was established. Production launch options require a uint Steam app ID and construct fixed steam://run/{id} or steam://install/{id} URLs. User-selected titles, collection names, manifest install directories, and downloaded app names do not become shell commands. WPF/Avalonia and Swift require an explicit launch/install action. Family-sharing classification affects selection and presentation; it does not bypass Steam's license enforcement.

resolvedQuestions.question: Do the automatic update paths accept an unauthenticated replacement binary by default?
resolvedQuestions.resolution: Linux checks a configured RSA public key against a signature binding version, download URL, and SHA-256, then verifies the downloaded binary hash. Missing keys reject updates unless unsigned feeds are explicitly enabled through a local environment setting. HTTPS is required except loopback HTTP. The pending marker is not authenticated again before application, but resides in the user's own application data directory; no lower-trust write route was found, so same-user marker manipulation is not a reportable vulnerability. Reverification at application time and constrained pending paths would strengthen future update work. Windows legacy Squirrel updates are disabled by default, and WPF startup does not call the updater. macOS updates are no-op. Official key provisioning and end-to-end release verification remain operational work.

resolvedQuestions.question: Are malformed Steam caches adequately bounded?
resolvedQuestions.resolution: There are concrete robustness and hardening gaps. C# binary parsing trusts string counts and decompressed-size declarations and lacks nesting limits; Swift numeric readers can slice past truncated buffers, and string-table offset arithmetic lacks complete bounds checks. Recursive text/metadata parsing also lacks explicit depth limits. These can produce allocation pressure or process failure on malformed inputs. Current production sources are the local Steam installation/cache; no repository-backed route lets a distinct lower-trust attacker supply arbitrary cache bytes. Consequently these are not promoted to security vulnerabilities. Add size/depth limits, checked numeric reads, type checks for cloud JSON, and malformed modern-format fixtures before introducing downloaded or imported cache sources.

resolvedQuestions.question: Does native library loading introduce an attacker-controlled execution path?
resolvedQuestions.resolution: Native candidates are explicitly constructed beneath the locally resolved Steam installation. Windows resolution reads the current user's Steam registry key; Linux uses validated local environment/home installation candidates. No remote metadata field supplies a native library path. Attacks requiring modification of the user's environment or trusted Steam installation were not treated as independent vulnerabilities. Native handles are reset and freed; successful Steam API initialization is tracked for shutdown.

resolvedQuestions.question: Are the experimental pipe and process-memory hooks active attack surfaces in the shipped clients?
resolvedQuestions.resolution: No production composition or client project references activate SteamHooks. The hooks are prototype library code. Windows memory access is read-only; Linux process-memory access additionally requires the explicit unsafe-read option and otherwise degrades to no-op. The named-pipe implementation lacks explicit message-size bounds, but there is no current shipped consumer connecting pipe events to privileged operations or game launching. Keep hooks outside normal discovery; reassess pipe authentication, message limits, lifecycle, and process identity if integrating them.

resolvedQuestions.question: Do telemetry, caches, or UI rendering expose secrets or executable content?
resolvedQuestions.resolution: No hardcoded credentials or source-backed secret exfiltration path was found. .NET telemetry defaults to disabled and uses consent checks with local file/debug sinks; the declared telemetry endpoint is unused. macOS diagnostics use local unified logging. Remote artwork uses fixed Steam/SteamDB URLs containing numeric app IDs; missing macOS names use the fixed Steam Store endpoint. Returned names and local metadata are rendered as text, without WebView/HTML execution. Persisted preferences and names use typed JSON or UserDefaults. Documentation describing privacy settings and onboarding is ahead of the actual UI and should be corrected; this is a product/documentation gap.

resolvedQuestions.question: Do CI and release scripts expose an untrusted pull request to publishing credentials?
resolvedQuestions.resolution: The ordinary pull-request workflow uses pull_request, not pull_request_target, and requests contents:read. Publishing occurs in the separate release/workflow-dispatch workflow. No source-backed PR-to-release credential crossing was found. The Linux release workflow downloads and executes a moving appimagetool continuous artifact without a pinned digest; pinning the tool and action revisions would reduce supply-chain exposure, but an upstream compromise was not assumed as an existing vulnerability. Shell packaging arguments and generated update paths are quoted. Release version input is passed through environment values rather than inserted directly into shell source.

resolvedQuestions.question: What security validation gaps remain despite the existing tests?
resolvedQuestions.resolution: Linux update tests include signed-feed success, invalid-key rejection, unsigned-feed rejection, and checksum failures, but return early on non-Linux systems. A Windows test-run pass count therefore does not execute those update assertions. C# binary parser coverage contains one legacy truncated-entry case; Swift parser tests use valid modern fixtures and do not exercise malformed offsets, truncated numeric values, nesting limits, or allocation bounds. Historical success claims in improvements.md and macOS checklists were treated as documentation, not current execution evidence.

surfaces.label: Local Steam VDF, binary appinfo, decompression and Swift parsing
surfaces.notes: Missing allocation/depth/truncation bounds are robustness improvements. No distinct lower-trust attacker route to Steam-managed local bytes was established. Parent reproduced correct parsing of 3,073 entries in the actual v41 appinfo; no exploit was executed.

partiallyReviewedFiles.evidence: Traced text/binary file entrypoints, local user selection, path construction, tree traversal, and exception containment; not claiming full-file coverage.
Traced local Steam discovery, manifest/config reads, user-directory inputs, and appinfo caller; not claiming full-file coverage.

resolvedQuestions.answer: Yes. TryReadHeader only checks eight remaining bytes before reading the additional eight-byte offset for versions 41/42. It then seeks to the supplied signed offset and allocates string[stringCount] without validating the offset, count against remaining bytes, or a resource budget. A negative offset can throw an ArgumentOutOfRangeException that the production fallback does not catch. A huge count can allocate excessive memory; EOF becomes an empty string and does not stop the count loop.

resolvedQuestions.question: Can a malformed modern appinfo string table exhaust resources or escape error recovery?
resolvedQuestions.security_boundary_resolution: No repository evidence that another principal can supply raw appinfo headers without already controlling the local Steam cache or process configuration. Same-user edits are not classified as an exploit.
resolvedQuestions.suggested_improvement: Validate the complete version-specific header, require an in-range nonnegative table offset, cap counts and bytes, require each declared string to terminate, and reject malformed data as InvalidDataException before allocation.

resolvedQuestions.answer: Entry end positions are checked against the stream length, malformed entry exceptions are skipped, and buffers are returned in finally blocks. The zstd envelope checks its minimum size, checksum agreement, footer marker, nonnegative decompressed size, exact decompression output length, and actual CRC. However, it rents the advertised decompressed-size buffer before validating the compressed frame or checksum contents, with no output cap. A small malformed envelope can therefore request an enormous allocation. CRC is an integrity check rather than authentication, but this code does not use it as authorization. No executable deserialization or input-selected code-loading sink was found.
counterevidence: Modern entry payload reads are bounded by the actual enclosing stream.
Legacy entries reject sizes greater than Int32.MaxValue and sizes exceeding remaining bytes at lines 398-412.
Decompressor.TryUnwrap writes into a supplied bounded destination; no raw attacker-controlled pointer is present.
The only production ParseAppInfo caller located is SteamVdfFallback's local cache load.
resolvedQuestions.question: Do entry and zstd safeguards prevent size-based exhaustion or code access?
resolvedQuestions.suggested_improvement: Apply explicit per-entry, decompressed-output, and aggregate parsing budgets before renting memory.

resolvedQuestions.answer: Yes. Text VDF, legacy binary VDF, modern KVObject conversion, the separate libraryfolders parser, and Mac text/binary parsing recursively descend without a depth limit. Mac text parsing and the separate .NET libraryfolders tokenizer also recurse for consecutive comments. A sufficiently deep local file can exhaust the stack; the surrounding catches or Swift try? do not contain stack exhaustion. Input advancement otherwise prevents a simple zero-progress parsing loop.
caller_evidence: SteamVdfFallback.cs:108-114,154-160,250-256,849-866 reads loginusers/localconfig/sharedconfig from the selected local Steam directory.
SteamLibraryService.swift:81-118,146-183,466-488 reads local Steam files; environment paths are converted to file URLs.
resolvedQuestions.question: Can deeply nested input defeat parser recovery?
resolvedQuestions.security_boundary_resolution: The public parsing APIs accept caller-supplied content, but no shipped deployment exposing them to a distinct untrusted principal was identified. Upstream Steam-publisher control over arbitrary serialized nesting was not established and is not assumed.
resolvedQuestions.suggested_improvement: Add a shared depth/node budget; replace comment recursion with iteration and consider iterative tree traversal.

resolvedQuestions.answer: Not consistently. readStringTable checks only offset + 4 <= data.count: a negative offset passes and reaches an invalid Data range, while Int.max can overflow the addition. It reserves the unbounded declared count before reading. parseObject validates the four-byte key index but reads a four-byte UInt32 value without checking that another four bytes remain, so a truncated scalar can trap despite valid outer entry lengths. These are process-crash robustness defects; Swift try? does not catch bounds/overflow traps.
resolvedQuestions.caller_evidence: SteamLibraryService.swift:597-599 passes the fixed local appcache/appinfo.vdf file URL.
counterevidence: Top-level reads require at least 16 bytes and a supported magic/version.
Outer entries validate entryEnd against data.count and metadataLength against entryEnd.
String table indices are validated before lookup at line 213.
Binary blob-length reads have an additional four-byte check at lines 237-242.
resolvedQuestions.question: Does Mac malformed appinfo handling fail safely?
resolvedQuestions.suggested_improvement: Use checked nonnegative ranges expressed as offset <= count - width; validate each primitive value read and bound table allocation.

resolvedQuestions.answer: Windows/Linux share the .NET implementation, which supports and validates the Valve zstd envelope. Mac explicitly skips zstd payloads at SteamAppInfoParser.swift:84-85, so the .NET zstd allocation issue does not apply there. Mac instead has direct Data-range/overflow traps. Both implementations lack overall size/depth budgets. The separate .NET libraryfolders parser and Mac text parser support comments; ValveTextVdfParser does not implement comment skipping.

resolvedQuestions.answer: The parser decodes UTF-8, splits lines/tabs, and uses TryParse for numeric fields. Its production caller clamps each snapshot read to 32–16384 bytes before parsing. LinuxProcMemReader independently applies the same clamp. Watched app IDs are filtered after parsing. No remote ingestion path or dangerous sink was found, so missing per-field limits are not a demonstrated denial-of-service vulnerability.

Keep hooks outside normal discovery; reassess pipe authentication, message limits, lifecycle, and process identity if integrating them.

resolvedQuestions.question: Do telemetry, caches, or UI rendering expose secrets or executable content?
resolvedQuestions.resolution: No hardcoded credentials or source-backed secret exfiltration path was found. .NET telemetry defaults to disabled and uses consent checks with local file/debug sinks; the declared telemetry endpoint is unused. macOS diagnostics use local unified logging. Remote artwork uses fixed Steam/SteamDB URLs containing numeric app IDs; missing macOS names use the fixed Steam Store endpoint. Returned names and local metadata are rendered as text, without WebView/HTML execution. Persisted preferences and names use typed JSON or UserDefaults. Documentation describing privacy settings and onboarding is ahead of the actual UI and should be corrected; this is a product/documentation gap.

resolvedQuestions.question: Do CI and release scripts expose an untrusted pull request to publishing credentials?
resolvedQuestions.resolution: The ordinary pull-request workflow uses pull_request, not pull_request_target, and requests contents:read. Publishing occurs in the separate release/workflow-dispatch workflow. No source-backed PR-to-release credential crossing was found. The Linux release workflow downloads and executes a moving appimagetool continuous artifact without a pinned digest; pinning the tool and action revisions would reduce supply-chain exposure, but an upstream compromise was not assumed as an existing vulnerability. Shell packaging arguments and generated update paths are quoted. Release version input is passed through environment values rather than inserted directly into shell source.

resolvedQuestions.question: What security validation gaps remain despite the existing tests?
resolvedQuestions.resolution: Linux update tests include signed-feed success, invalid-key rejection, unsigned-feed rejection, and checksum failures, but return early on non-Linux systems. A Windows test-run pass count therefore does not execute those update assertions. C# binary parser coverage contains one legacy truncated-entry case; Swift parser tests use valid modern fixtures and do not exercise malformed offsets, truncated numeric values, nesting limits, or allocation bounds. Historical success claims in improvements.md and macOS checklists were treated as documentation, not current execution evidence.
